equation_request.abstract: Quantum walks have been very useful in developing search algorithms in quantum information, in particular for devising of spatial search algorithms. However, the construction of continuous-time quantum search algorithms in two-dimensional lattices has proved difficult, requiring additional degrees of freedom. Here, we demonstrate that continuous-time quantum walk search is possible in two-dimensions by changing the search topology to a graphene lattice, utilising the Dirac point in the energy spectrum. This is made possible by making a change to standard methods of marking a particular site in the lattice. Various ways of marking a site are shown to result in successful search protocols. We further establish that the search can be adapted to transfer probability amplitude across the lattice between specific lattice sites thus establishing a line of communication between these sites.

specification.problem: Continuous-time quantum walk (CTQW) spatial search for a single marked site on a two-dimensional honeycomb (graphene) lattice, exploiting the Dirac point (E=0) of the tight-binding spectrum, with the marked site identified by a modified (non-standard) local perturbation of the walk Hamiltonian rather than only an on-site potential.
specification.reconstruction_scope: One smallest useful construction: nearest-neighbour tight-binding CTQW on an n x n periodic honeycomb lattice with N = 2 n^2 sites, n = 3 (N = 18 sites, so that Dirac-point momenta are allowed), a single marked site w, a bond-plus-on-site marking perturbation with free strengths, an initial state built from the E = 0 (Dirac-point) Bloch eigenstates, time evolution, and computational-basis measurement to estimate the success probability at w as a function of time. Outside scope: the paper's specific catalogue of 'various ways of marking a site', the paper's asymptotic scaling claims (search time / success probability versus N), the comparison showing failure of standard marking on square lattices, and the amplitude-transfer (communication) protocol between two sites.

symbols.meaning: Linear size of the periodic honeycomb lattice in unit cells; n must be a multiple of 3 for the Dirac points to be allowed momenta
Total number of lattice sites, N = 2 n^2
Site label: unit-cell coordinates m_1, m_2 and sublattice index sigma (A = 0, B = 1)
Nearest-neighbour hopping strength of the unperturbed walk Hamiltonian
Unperturbed tight-binding (adjacency-type) CTQW Hamiltonian on the honeycomb lattice

symbols.domain: w \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}; instance w = index of (0,0,A) = 0

symbols.meaning: Set of the three nearest neighbours of w
Strengths of the bond modification and on-site potential forming the marking perturbation
Bloch phases along the two lattice directions, \theta_i = 2\pi q_i / n
Probability of finding the walker at the marked site at time t
Integer encoding of a site into the computational basis of the site register

equations.label: Unperturbed graphene CTQW Hamiltonian
equations.latex: H_0 = -\gamma \sum_{m_1, m_2 \in \mathbb{Z}_n} \sum_{\delta \in \{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\}} \left( |m_1, m_2, A\rangle\langle m_1 - \delta_1, m_2 - \delta_2, B| + \mathrm{h.c.} \right)
equations.description: Nearest-neighbour hopping on the periodic honeycomb lattice: site (m_1,m_2,A) couples to B sites in cells (m_1,m_2), (m_1-1,m_2), (m_1,m_2-1), indices taken mod n. This is the walk generator (Laplacian and adjacency generators coincide up to a constant on this 3-regular graph).
equations.abstract_quote: continuous-time quantum walk search is possible in two-dimensions by changing the search topology to a graphene lattice
equations.justification: A CTQW on a graphene lattice is generated by the nearest-neighbour tight-binding/adjacency Hamiltonian of the honeycomb graph; the abstract names the walk type and the lattice but not the explicit matrix, so this is an inference.
assumptions: Uniform hopping gamma and zero on-site energy assumed

equations.label: Spectrum and Dirac point of H_0
equations.description: Two-band Bloch spectrum of the honeycomb tight-binding model; the two bands touch at E = 0 at the two inequivalent Dirac points K, K', which are allowed momenta exactly when 3 divides n. At these momenta the sublattice-pure Bloch states |K,A>, |K,B>, |K',A>, |K',B> are exact zero-energy eigenstates of H_0.
equations.justification: Standard tight-binding result for graphene; the abstract states that the Dirac point is utilised but gives no formula.

equations.label: Marked (search) Hamiltonian with modified local marking
equations.description: The marked site is distinguished by changing the three bonds attached to it (hopping -gamma becomes -gamma + epsilon) and optionally adding an on-site potential mu. The standard CTQW marking corresponds to epsilon = 0, mu != 0; the abstract states that a change to this standard marking is required and that several variants work.
equations.abstract_quote: This is made possible by making a change to standard methods of marking a particular site in the lattice. Various ways of marking a site are shown to result in successful search protocols.
equations.justification: The abstract asserts that a non-standard local marking is used and that several variants succeed; a local perturbation acting on the marked site and its bonds is the natural general form. The specific (epsilon, mu) values and the exact family of perturbations used in the paper are not given in the abstract and are treated as a parameter scan.
assumptions: Perturbation is supported on w and its three bonds only
Specific values of epsilon and mu are not established by the abstract; the instance scans epsilon in (0, gamma] with mu in {0, -gamma}

equations.label: Initial state at the Dirac point
equations.latex: |\psi(0)\rangle = \sqrt{\frac{2}{N}} \sum_{m_1, m_2 \in \mathbb{Z}_n} \cos\!\left( \frac{2\pi (m_1 - m_2)}{3} \right) \left( |m_1, m_2, A\rangle + |m_1, m_2, B\rangle \right), \qquad H_0 |\psi(0)\rangle = 0
equations.description: A real, normalised, equal-weight superposition of the four zero-energy Dirac-point Bloch states (K and K', both sublattices). It lies in the E = 0 eigenspace of H_0, so the search dynamics are driven by the coupling of the perturbation to the Dirac-point states rather than to the band bottom (which the uniform superposition would occupy).
equations.justification: The abstract says the Dirac point is utilised but does not specify the starting state; this is one concrete choice of a delocalised zero-energy state. Normalisation: (2/N) * 2 * sum_cells cos^2 = (2/N) * 2 * (n^2/2) = 1 for 3 | n.
assumptions: The paper's actual starting state may differ (e.g. a single Dirac Bloch state or a differently weighted combination)

equations.label: Time evolution and success probability
equations.latex: |\psi(t)\rangle = e^{-i H_w t} |\psi(0)\rangle, \qquad P_w(t) = \left| \langle w | \psi(t) \rangle \right|^2, \qquad t_{\mathrm{opt}} = \arg\max_{t \in [0, T]} P_w(t)
equations.description: Continuous-time evolution under the marked Hamiltonian and the probability of locating the walker at the marked site; the search time is the first (or global, within a finite window T) maximum of P_w(t). Probability on the neighbours N(w) may also be monitored since a bond perturbation can localise amplitude on w and its neighbours jointly.
equations.justification: Definition of CTQW search success probability; no closed form for t_opt or max P_w is claimed here since the abstract gives no scaling result.
assumptions: Finite time window T chosen numerically, e.g. T = 10 sqrt(N)/gamma for the instance

equations.label: Site-to-qubit encoding for the instance
equations.latex: \mathrm{idx}(m_1, m_2, \sigma) = 2(n m_1 + m_2) + \sigma, \qquad |m_1, m_2, \sigma\rangle \mapsto |\mathrm{idx}\rangle_{\lceil \log_2 N \rceil}, \qquad \langle k | H_w | l \rangle = 0 \ \text{for } k \ge N \text{ or } l \ge N
equations.description: Binary encoding of the N = 18 sites into a 5-qubit register (little-endian integer), with the 14 unused basis states decoupled (zero rows/columns of H_w).
equations.justification: Needed so that the equations map unambiguously onto a circuit; the paper describes a physical walk, not a qubit encoding.
assumptions: Binary (not one-hot) encoding chosen for minimal qubit count

registers.name: site
registers.role: Holds the walker position |idx(m_1,m_2,sigma)> in binary; amplitudes on basis states 18..31 are identically zero

specification.initial_state: |psi(0)> as in eq_4: the normalised real Dirac-point superposition sqrt(2/N) sum_{m1,m2} cos(2 pi (m1 - m2)/3) (|m1,m2,A> + |m1,m2,B>), prepared on the site register via a generic 18-amplitude state preparation (amplitudes take values in {+sqrt(2/N), -sqrt(2/N)/2}).

steps.description: Fix the instance: n = 3, N = 18, gamma = 1, periodic honeycomb adjacency per eq_1, marked site w = idx(0,0,A) = 0 with neighbours N(w) = {idx(0,0,B), idx(2,0,B), idx(0,2,B)}; build H_w for chosen (epsilon, mu) per eq_3 and embed it in the 5-qubit space per eq_6.
Prepare the Dirac-point initial state |psi(0)> (eq_4) on the site register; verify classically that H_0 |psi(0)> = 0 using eq_2.

Apply U(t) = exp(-i H_w t) for a grid of times t in [0, T] (exact unitary synthesis or a Trotter product of the bond terms; each bond term is a 2-level X-type coupling between two computational basis states).

Measure the site register in the computational basis and estimate P_w(t) (and optionally the total probability on N(w)); repeat the time scan for each (epsilon, mu) in the chosen parameter set and record t_opt and max P_w.

specification.measurement: Computational-basis measurement of the 5-qubit site register; the empirical frequency of outcome idx(w) = 0 estimates P_w(t). Optionally also record frequencies of the three neighbour indices.
specification.classical_postprocessing: For each perturbation setting (epsilon, mu), locate the time t_opt maximising the estimated P_w(t) over the scanned grid and report (t_opt, P_w(t_opt)); compare against the unperturbed dynamics (epsilon = mu = 0), for which P_w(t) stays at O(1/N), and against the standard on-site-only marking (epsilon = 0) to check that bond modification is what enables localisation. No asymptotic scaling in N is claimed from the single instance.
assumptions: No experiment_scope was supplied; the n = 3 (N = 18 site) periodic honeycomb instance with one marked site is a chosen smallest useful construction
Periodic boundary conditions and uniform hopping gamma = 1 with zero on-site energy
Marking perturbation restricted to the marked site and its three bonds, with strengths (epsilon, mu) treated as scan parameters rather than paper-sourced values
Initial state chosen as a real equal-weight combination of the four E = 0 Dirac-point Bloch states; the paper's choice is unknown
Binary site encoding on 5 qubits with unused basis states decoupled
The amplitude-transfer/communication protocol between two sites and the paper's scaling results are explicitly outside the reconstructed scope
missing_information: Exact definitions of the 'various ways of marking a site' used in the paper and their perturbation strengths
The paper's choice of initial state and whether it is a Dirac-point state or another delocalised state
Boundary conditions and lattice sizes used in the paper
Quantitative results: scaling of optimal search time and success probability with N, and any logarithmic corrections
Construction of the amplitude-transfer protocol between two specific sites (presumably two marked sites with a symmetric perturbation), including its timing and fidelity
Any analytic (e.g. perturbative or reduced two/four-level) model the paper uses to explain localisation at the Dirac point
